newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: European cocoa buyers await new crop arrivals.
newsitem.headline: European cocoa buyers await new crop arrivals.

text.p: Europe's physical cocoa trade remains at a low ebb with industry interest thin and the market still looking ahead to the first arrivals from African origins.
Traders reported only scant demand from chocolate manufacturers this week, saying their position over the future direction of the market had not changed.
"We've seen small bits of buying but nothing substantial. Apart from the pick-up in activity a couple of weeks ago, it's been like this for months," one trader said on Thursday.
London futures have also meandered this week, the benchmark December holding around 975 stg a tonne.
Traders said sterling's appreciation against the guilder in recent weeks had been an additional dampener on demand.

The main focus for the trade continued to be the size and timing of African crops. Traders said there were no fresh developments on estimates and said today's ED&F Man estimate of a 36,000 tonne surplus in the current season had little impact.

The Cameroon crop was starting to arrive from up country and the Nigerian one was expected in the next few weeks, traders said. Weather reports in the region were favourable and the crops were described as "average to good" in terms of size.

But the size and timing of the main Ivorian harvest will determine the direction of prices in the medium term. Traders said forecasts were continuing to centre on 900,000 tonnes and above, around 100,000 more than initial estimates.

The repercussions of the attempted September squeeze were still the subject of debate and one trader said the depressed levels of nearby futures indicated market opinion favoured the early release of the delivered cocoa.
But it was still seen as a major imponderable hanging over the market and one which may finally have little to do with cocoa.
"The decisions being taken on what to do probably have more to do with the financial considerations of a major company than market fundamentals and that makes it more difficult to predict," he said.
